etymology: From the surname Calamy; the leading Presbyterian divine of the Westminster Assembly, ejected in 1662.
biblical_def: Edmund Calamy was one of the chief Presbyterian divines of the Westminster Assembly, a leading preacher of London and a champion of the Reformed ordering of the church. He was one of the five authors of the famous tract Smectymnuus, which defended the Presbyterian government of elders against the claims of prelacy, holding that the New Testament knows the elder, set in order by the laying on of the hands of the presbytery (1Ti 4:14), as the one ordinary office of rule in the church, the pastor charged to feed the flock of God and take the oversight thereof (1Pe 5:2). At the Restoration he could not conform, and was among the two thousand ministers ejected in sixteen hundred and sixty-two. The dictionary honours Calamy as a faithful divine of the Assembly and a steadfast nonconformist, who laboured to set the church in order according to the word, ordaining elders in every city as the apostle had appointed (Tit 1:5). He held that the government of Christ’s church is not left to the wisdom of men but given in the Scriptures, and that the rule of elders, not the lordship of prelates, is the New Testament pattern. He stands among the Westminster worthies who gave the church its great confession and catechisms, and who suffered for the truth they had confessed.
webster_summary: A leading Presbyterian divine of the Westminster Assembly and a Smectymnuus author, ejected in 1662.

corruption_summary: He defended the New Testament government of elders against prelacy, and suffered ejection rather than conform against conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Calamy opposed was the lordly prelacy that set bishops over the church as a separate and superior order, against the New Testament pattern of the eldership. With his fellow authors of Smectymnuus he showed from the Scriptures that the elder is the one ordinary office of rule, and that the government of the church is not a matter of human policy but of divine appointment. The dictionary honours this defence of Christ’s ordering of His church.

What is honourable in Calamy is his faithful labour at the Assembly and his costly nonconformity. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the government of the church is given in the word, not left to the will of men. He held that elders, not prelates, are the New Testament rule; and when the Restoration required conformity his conscience could not yield, he chose ejection with his brethren. The Westminster worthies gave the church its great confession, and many of them sealed it with the loss of all they had.

etymology: From the surname Marshall; the great preacher of the Long Parliament and a divine of the Westminster Assembly.
biblical_def: Stephen Marshall was among the most influential preachers of his age, a divine of the Westminster Assembly and the foremost pulpit voice before the Long Parliament in the years of the civil war. His sermon Meroz Cursed, preached again and again before the Parliament and the armies, took up the angel’s word in the song of Deborah, Curse ye Meroz, because they came not to the help of the LORD against the mighty (Jdg 5:23), to rouse a slumbering people to the cause of reformation. He was one of the five authors of Smectymnuus and a tireless labourer in the Assembly that framed the Confession and Catechisms. The dictionary honours Marshall as a preacher who set the word of God before rulers and nations, reminding the judges of the land that they judge not for man, but for the LORD (2Ch 19:6), and who counted the work of reformation a great work from which he would not come down (Neh 6:3). His preaching moved a kingdom, for good and sometimes beyond what later wisdom would approve; yet his aim was the honour of God and the reforming of the church, and he stands among the Westminster divines whose labours gave the Reformed churches their fullest confession of the faith.

corruption_summary: He roused a slumbering people to the cause of reformation and set the word of God before rulers and nations.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Marshall preached against was the slothful neutrality of those who would not stir for the cause of God, the men of Meroz who came not to the help of the LORD against the mighty. He summoned a slumbering people to the work of reformation, and reminded the rulers of the land that they judge not for man but for the LORD. The dictionary honours this prophetic boldness that set the word of God before the highest powers.

What is honourable in Marshall is the seriousness with which he held the cause of God before a nation. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the work of reformation is a great work, not to be left undone while men dwell at ease in their cieled houses. His preaching moved a kingdom, and not in every particular as later wisdom would approve; yet his aim was the honour of God and the reforming of the church, and he laboured faithfully in the Assembly that gave the Reformed churches their fullest confession of the faith.

etymology: From the surname Twisse; the first prolocutor (moderator) of the Westminster Assembly and a learned defender of predestination.
biblical_def: William Twisse was the first prolocutor, or moderator, of the Westminster Assembly, chosen for the office for his great learning and his weight among the divines. He was a profound and subtle theologian, a stout defender of the doctrines of sovereign grace and of predestination, who held with full conviction the eternal purpose of God in election. He taught that the purpose of God according to election stands not of works, but of him that calleth, settled before the children were born or had done good or evil (Rom 9:11); that God predestinated His people unto the adoption of children according to the good pleasure of His will (Eph 1:5); and that the golden chain is unbroken, for whom He did predestinate, them He also called, justified, and glorified (Rom 8:30). The dictionary honours Twisse as the learned moderator under whom the Assembly began its great work, and as a faithful champion of the sovereignty of God in salvation, who confessed with the apostle that of him, and through him, and to him, are all things, to whom be glory for ever (Rom 11:36). He stands at the head of the Assembly that gave the Reformed churches the Westminster Confession, a monument to the doctrines of grace he so ably defended.
webster_summary: The first moderator of the Westminster Assembly and a learned defender of predestination and sovereign grace.

corruption_summary: He defended the eternal purpose of God in election against every doctrine that made salvation rest on the will of man.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Twisse withstood was the Arminian and Pelagian denial of God’s sovereign purpose in election, which would make the choice of salvation rest at last upon the will of man. Against this he held the eternal decree of God, the purpose according to election that stands not of works but of Him that calleth, settled before the foundation of the world. The dictionary honours his learned defence of the sovereignty of God in salvation.

What is honourable in Twisse is the union of deep learning and full conviction in the doctrines of grace. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the sovereignty of God in election. The golden chain is His, from predestination to glory, and no link is forged by man; of Him and through Him and to Him are all things. As first moderator of the Assembly that gave the church the Westminster Confession, Twisse stands at the fountainhead of that great labour, a faithful witness to the free and sovereign grace of God.

etymology: From the surname Preston; the Puritan divine, master of Emmanuel College and preacher of the covenant of grace.
biblical_def: John Preston was a Puritan divine of the early seventeenth century, master of Emmanuel College in Cambridge and one of the most powerful preachers of his day, who carried the gospel even into the court of King James and King Charles. His chief theme was the covenant of grace and the life of faith, set forth in his books The New Covenant and The Breastplate of Faith and Love. He preached the everlasting covenant that God establishes with His people and their seed, to be a God unto them (Gen 17:7), the new covenant in which the Lord writes His laws upon the heart and is their God and they His people (Heb 8:10). He pressed home that the blessing of Abraham comes upon the Gentiles through Christ, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith (Gal 3:14), and that to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness (Rom 4:5). The dictionary honours Preston as a master of covenant theology and a preacher who drew sinners to rest upon the free grace of God in Christ. He taught the troubled soul to look not to its own worthiness but to the covenant and the promise, and to take hold of God by faith as a God in covenant who cannot deny Himself.
webster_summary: A Puritan divine and master of Emmanuel College, a powerful preacher of the covenant of grace and the life of faith.

corruption_summary: He preached the covenant of grace and the life of faith, drawing sinners to rest on God’s free promise, not their own worth.
corruption_paragraphs: The error Preston preached against was the bondage of a religion of works and the despair of a soul looking to its own worthiness. He set before sinners the covenant of grace, the everlasting covenant in which God binds Himself to be a God to His people and to write His law upon their hearts. The dictionary honours this covenant theology, which casts the trembling soul wholly upon the free promise of God in Christ.

What is honourable in Preston is that he made the covenant the ground of faith and assurance. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the believer rests not on his own worthiness but on the God who justifieth the ungodly, whose faith is counted for righteousness. Preston taught the troubled to take hold of God by faith as a God in covenant who cannot deny Himself, and so to find peace not in themselves but in the promise. This is the very marrow of the gospel the Reformation recovered.

etymology: From the surname Greenham; the Elizabethan Puritan pastor of Dry Drayton, a pioneer of the cure of troubled souls.
biblical_def: Richard Greenham was an Elizabethan Puritan, pastor of the village of Dry Drayton near Cambridge, remembered as one of the first masters of the cure of souls, the careful and tender dealing with troubled and afflicted consciences. He rose before dawn to preach to his people in the fields, and he was sought from far and near by those whose spirits were wounded with the sense of sin or cast down with doubt and despair. He had, as the prophet says, the tongue of the learned, to know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary (Isa 50:4). The dictionary honours Greenham as a spiritual physician who pointed the heavy-laden to Christ, who says, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Mat 11:28). He knew that a wounded spirit who can bear (Pro 18:14), and that the God of all comfort comforts His people in their tribulation, that they may comfort others by the comfort wherewith they themselves are comforted of God (2Co 1:4). His casuistry, the patient applying of the Scriptures to the particular cases of the conscience, opened a path that the great Puritan physicians of the soul, Perkins, Sibbes, and Bolton, walked after him. He teaches the pastor to deal gently and wisely with the broken, binding up where the world only wounds.

corruption_summary: He pioneered the tender cure of troubled souls, pointing the heavy-laden to the rest that is in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Greenham is the tenderness and wisdom of his dealing with afflicted consciences. In an age that often left the wounded soul to itself, he made it his special labour to bind up the broken-hearted, applying the Scriptures to the particular case of each troubled spirit. The dictionary honours this cure of souls as a true and needful part of the pastor’s work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the pastoral cure of the conscience, the speaking of a word in season to him that is weary. The dictionary marks that this is no therapy of the world’s sort, which soothes the sinner without naming his sin, but the bringing of the heavy-laden to Christ, who alone gives rest, and the comforting of the afflicted with the comfort of God. Greenham opened a path the great Puritan physicians of the soul walked after him, teaching the pastor to deal gently with the broken and to bind up where the world only wounds.

etymology: From the surname Hildersham; a leading Puritan preacher and expositor, often suspended for nonconformity.
biblical_def: Arthur Hildersham was a leading Puritan preacher of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, an expositor of great power whose Lectures upon the fifty-first Psalm and upon the fourth chapter of John were long treasured by the godly. He was again and again suspended and silenced for his nonconformity, refusing to bind his ministry to ceremonies the word of God had not commanded, yet returning to preach whenever the door was opened. He held with the apostles that we ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29), and knew that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2Ti 3:12). His exposition of the penitential psalm pressed home that the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart, which God will not despise (Psa 51:17), and his lectures on John’s Gospel that God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24). The dictionary honours Hildersham as a faithful and suffering preacher of the word, who counted the favour of God above the favour of the bishops, and the cleanness of conscience above the ease of conformity. His patient endurance under silencing teaches that the minister’s first loyalty is to the word of God, and that to preach the truth at the cost of office is itself a sermon.

corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Hildersham resisted was the imposing upon the worship and ministry of the church of ceremonies the word of God had not commanded. Holding the regulative principle, he would not conform, and was repeatedly suspended and silenced for it. The dictionary honours his nonconformity, the patient endurance that obeyed God rather than men and counted the cleanness of conscience above the ease of office.

What is honourable in Hildersham is his union of powerful exposition and faithful suffering. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the minister’s first loyalty is to the word of God, not to the will of the bishops. He preached the broken and contrite heart God will not despise, and the worship of God in spirit and in truth; and when silenced he returned to preach whenever he could. His endurance teaches that to preach the truth at the cost of office is itself a sermon, and that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.

etymology: From the surname Gataker; a learned divine of the Westminster Assembly and a defender of the doctrine of providence.
biblical_def: Thomas Gataker was a divine of the Westminster Assembly and one of the most learned men of his time, a classical scholar of European fame and a careful theologian. Among his labours was a defence of the doctrine of providence against the superstition of his age, which would read the will of God in the casting of lots, the stars, and other vain divinations. Gataker showed that while the lot is cast into the lap, the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33), so that nothing is by chance, yet men may not pry into God’s secret will by forbidden arts. He held that a man’s heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps (Pro 16:9), and that not a sparrow falls to the ground without the Father (Mat 10:29). The dictionary honours Gataker as a learned defender of the Reformed doctrine of providence, who steered between the two errors of a blind chance that denies God’s government and a prying superstition that seeks His secret will by unlawful means. He taught the believer to rest in the all-disposing hand of God, to say with Job, The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21), and to leave the hidden things to God while walking by the revealed word.

corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Gataker confronted was twofold: the denial of God’s government in the name of chance, and the prying superstition that sought His secret will by lots and stars and divination. He held the Reformed mean, that the lot and the sparrow alike are in the hand of God, so that nothing is by chance, yet men may not seek the hidden things by forbidden arts. The dictionary honours this learned defence of the doctrine of providence.

What is honourable in Gataker is the wisdom that steered between two errors. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of providence, which neither leaves the world to blind fortune nor pries into the secret counsel of God. The lot is cast into the lap, but its disposing is of the LORD; a man deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps. The believer is taught to rest in the all-disposing hand of God, to bless His name in giving and taking, and to walk by the revealed word while leaving the hidden things to Him.

etymology: From the surname Palmer; a divine of the Westminster Assembly noted for his gift in catechizing the young.
biblical_def: Herbert Palmer was a divine of the Westminster Assembly, a man of scrupulous piety and rare gift in the catechizing of children and the simple. He was esteemed the best catechist of his day, and his little book of questions and answers helped to shape the Assembly’s own labour upon the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, by which the Reformed faith has been taught to the young for centuries. The dictionary honours Palmer for this work of teaching the household and the church the first principles of the faith, after the charge of Moses, that the words of God be taught diligently unto the children, and talked of in the house and by the way, when we lie down and when we rise up (Deu 6:7). He laboured to train up a child in the way he should go, that when he is old he will not depart from it (Pro 22:6), and to make the young know the holy Scriptures from a child, which are able to make them wise unto salvation through faith in Christ (2Ti 3:15). Fathers are to bring up their children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4); and Palmer gave the church a method to do it. His catechizing teaches that the faith is not left to chance or feeling but handed down by patient instruction, that the children of the covenant may grow up knowing what they believe and why.

corruption_summary: He gave the church a method of catechizing, that the faith might be handed down to the young by patient instruction.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Palmer is his gift for catechizing, the patient teaching of children and the simple in the first principles of the faith. In an age that, like every age, was tempted to leave the young untaught, Palmer made it his special labour to instruct them, and his work fed the Assembly’s own great catechisms. The dictionary honours this teaching of the household and the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the catechizing of the young, the handing down of the faith by patient instruction rather than by chance or feeling. God charged Israel to teach His words diligently to their children; the wise man bids us train up a child in the way he should go; and Timothy knew the holy Scriptures from a child. Palmer gave the church a method to obey these charges, that the children of the covenant might grow up knowing what they believe and why, and so be furnished against the errors of their day.

etymology: From the names Obadiah, “servant of the LORD,” and the surname Sedgwick; a Westminster divine and searching preacher of the heart.
biblical_def: Obadiah Sedgwick was a divine of the Westminster Assembly and a searching preacher of London, whose books, among them The Anatomy of Secret Sins and The Doctrine of Providence, dig deep into the hidden recesses of the human heart. His special labour was to uncover the secret sins that men hide from others and from themselves, and to bring them into the light of God’s countenance. He pressed home the Psalmist’s prayer, Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults (Psa 19:12), and the awful truth that God has set our iniquities before Him, our secret sins in the light of His countenance (Psa 90:8). The dictionary honours Sedgwick as a faithful anatomist of the heart, who would not let the sinner rest in a fair outside while corruption nested within. He taught that there is no creature hid from the sight of God, but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13), and that the Lord at His coming will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts (1Co 4:5). His searching divinity teaches that true repentance reaches to the secret sins, and that the heart known to God must be known and judged by its owner, lest the hidden corruption undo him.

corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Sedgwick laid bare was the secret sin, the hidden corruption that men conceal from others and even from themselves while keeping a fair outside. He would not let the sinner rest in a clean exterior while sin nested in the heart, but brought the hidden things into the light of God’s countenance. The dictionary honours this searching divinity, which deals with the heart as God sees it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that true repentance reaches to the secret sins. There is no creature hid from the sight of God; all things are naked and opened to His eyes, and the Lord at His coming will bring to light the hidden things of darkness. Sedgwick teaches that the heart known to God must be known and judged by its owner, lest the hidden corruption undo him. This is no morbid introspection but the honest dealing of the soul with its God, who searches the heart and tries the reins.

etymology: From the surname Dickson; a Scottish Reformed divine and professor, co-author of The Sum of Saving Knowledge.
biblical_def: David Dickson was a Scottish Reformed divine of the seventeenth century, a preacher under whom revival came at Irvine, and afterward professor of divinity at Glasgow and Edinburgh. With James Durham he drew up The Sum of Saving Knowledge, a brief and warm statement of the covenant of grace and the way of salvation, which was bound with the Westminster Confession in Scotland and used of God to the conversion of many, among them later the great Thomas Boston. His Therapeutica Sacra dealt tenderly with the cases of conscience and the troubles of the believing soul, and his plain commentaries on the Psalms and the Epistles fed the godly. The dictionary honours Dickson as a faithful Scottish theologian and a physician of the soul, who set before troubled believers the everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure (2Sa 23:5), and the full assurance of faith. He taught the doubting to say with Paul, I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him (2Ti 1:12), and to rest in the truth that there is now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The hope of the saints is an anchor of the soul, sure and stedfast, entering within the veil (Heb 6:19); and Dickson’s labour was to make that anchor hold.

corruption_summary: He set before troubled believers the everlasting covenant and the full assurance of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Dickson is his union of sound theology and tender pastoral care. With Durham he gave the Scottish church The Sum of Saving Knowledge, a warm and clear statement of the covenant of grace by which many were converted; and in his Therapeutica Sacra he dealt gently with the troubles of the believing soul. The dictionary honours this labour of building up the saints in faith and assurance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the full assurance of faith resting on the everlasting covenant. Dickson set before the doubting the covenant ordered in all things and sure, and taught them to say with Paul, I know whom I have believed. The believer’s peace rests not on the changing frames of his heart but on the unchanging covenant of God; his hope is an anchor of the soul, sure and stedfast, entering within the veil. Dickson’s labour was to make that anchor hold, and to bring the troubled saint to rest in the no-condemnation that is in Christ Jesus.
